composition: Binary Fe-Al alloy with a nominal 16 at.% Al; the real composition determined by ICP is 16.0 at.% Al (8.4 wt.-%), the balance being Fe. The alloy was made for purity control with only low unavoidable impurity contents: 45 wt.ppm C, 40 wt.ppm Si and 60 wt.ppm O. A companion monocrystal of the same family had a nominal 17 at.% Al (real 16.8 at.%, 8.9 wt.-%, with 70 wt.ppm C, 140 wt.ppm Si, 50 wt.ppm Cu, 90 wt.ppm Mo). Aluminium is the sole alloying element and serves as the bcc substitutional solid-solution former responsible for solid-solution hardening, density reduction and the outset of short-range ordering in the iron matrix; the C content of this particular crystal (45 wt.ppm) is low enough that no carbides were detected in it.
conclusions: In the 1100 °C FC RT condition the Fe-16%Al monocrystal is a low-order, near-equilibrium reference state: it is essentially as hard (HU ≈2000 N/mm²) and as strong in compression (plateau ≈470–480 MPa) as the as-grown and other non-quenched conditions, confirming that short-range ordering has no major effect on the mechanical behaviour of these alloys and that only heat treatments above 600 °C (i.e. quenching) significantly modify it. The paper's wider conclusions place this sample in context: the room-temperature yield stress rises linearly with Al content up to 18 at.% by solid-solution hardening, ductility falls correspondingly with a ductile-to-brittle transition in the range 15–18 at.% Al at room temperature, quenching-produced excess vacancies contribute to hardening and to embrittlement (and heal out only slowly), and low-temperature yield-stress drops are attributed to mobile-dislocation/vacancy interaction while low-temperature deformation twinning arises from insufficient dislocation mobility, favoured by low temperature and high Al content. The study is significant because it separates real solid-solution and vacancy effects from short-range-ordering effects in high-purity (<100 wt.ppm C) Fe-Al alloys relevant to low-density, oxidation-resistant structural materials.
mechanisms: Short-range ordering (which reaches its maximum in Fe-Al at about 250 °C and is nearly completely suppressed by quenching from 1100 °C) does not control the hardness or flow stress of Fe-16%Al: the 1100 °C FC RT state, the 1100 °C FC 600 °C Q state, maximum-order 250 °C/14 d anneals and as-grown crystals all give essentially the same HU (≈2000 N/mm²) and similar stress-strain curves, so heat treatment below 600 °C has no major impact on deformation behaviour.

Annealing at a high temperature such as 1100 °C generates thermal vacancies, whose trapping depends on the cooling path: slow furnace cooling allows the excess-vacancy concentration to relax towards near-equilibrium, which is why the 1100 °C FC RT crystal sits at the low-hardness/low-flow-stress end of the series, while the hardest condition is the one quenched from 1100 °C.

Excess vacancies are immobile at low temperature and act as obstacles to dislocation movement, producing hardening and reduced ductility; their elimination by annealing is a slow process because of the high vacancy migration enthalpy in Fe-Al, so even a 300 °C/14 d anneal does not fully restore the quenched state.

The room-temperature yield stress of Fe-Al increases linearly with Al content up to 18 at.% (hardening coefficient ≈2.2 GPa in the present polycrystalline data, rate- and temperature-insensitive), matching Suzuki's theory of solid-solution hardening for bcc alloys; this Al solid-solution hardening is the primary source of strengthening, with short-range ordering playing only a minor role.

Increasing Al content reduces dislocation mobility, and quenched-in excess vacancies reduce it further; a reduced mobility of screw dislocations is a prerequisite for twin formation in bcc crystals, so decreasing dislocation mobility (by higher Al content and lower temperature) lowers the fracture strain and ultimately promotes brittle fracture without necking and deformation twinning.
microstructure: The material is a single crystal of Fe-16%Al with no grain boundaries; a single bcc Fe-Al solid-solution matrix phase is present, its degree of short-range order depending on prior heat treatment. The 1100 °C FC RT condition represents the minimum-degree-of-order, near-equilibrium vacancy state produced by slow cooling. Owing to the absence of grain boundaries the notion of grain size does not apply. The hardness specimens were (111)-oriented and the compression specimens [112]-oriented. The crystal contains rare, globular AlN inclusions with diameters up to 30 µm (identified by EDX); no carbides were detected in this Fe-16%Al monocrystal with 45 ppm C, even after a 14-day anneal at 320 °C, whereas thin plate-like/rod-like carbides appear on grain boundaries only in polycrystals (and in the Fe-17%Al monocrystal after 320 °C/14 d under 100 MPa load) owing to their higher carbon content (up to 80 ppm).
processing: The alloy was prepared by vacuum induction melting of zone-melted Fe (99.99% purity) and Al (99.999% purity) in Al2O3 crucibles, with solidification in Cu moulds into rods of usually 18 mm diameter. Monocrystals up to 10 cm long were then grown from these rods by the Bridgman method at a pulling rate of 10–15 mm/h, the growth plus subsequent cooling taking about 12 h. The crystals were etched in ammonium persulfate and oriented with a special laser light-figure method. Specimens were cut by electrostatic discharge machining and mechanically polished; monocrystal surfaces were finally polished with 3 µm diamond paste before testing (monocrystals were exempt from the ultrasonic acetone cleansing applied to other specimens). The defining heat treatment was 1100 °C, held usually for only 15 min, inside an evacuated (10^-6 bar) SiO2 capsule (no Si uptake was detected under these conditions), followed by furnace cooling to room temperature — the "1100 °C FC RT" state. This treatment belongs to a broader heat-treatment series (up to 600 °C for <14 days, higher temperatures for <4 days) used to vary the state of atomic order; heat treatments above 300 °C were all conducted in evacuated SiO2 capsules, and short treatments up to 300 °C in 99.99% pure argon.
properties: Universal microhardness HU of the (111)-oriented monocrystal in the 1100 °C FC RT state is ≈2000 N/mm², measured at room temperature with a Fischerscope H100 tester at a maximum load of 1 N and expressed as HU = F/(26.43·h²) [N/mm²] as averages of more than 40 measurements; across the whole heat-treatment series the HU values vary by at most about 10%, and the 1100 °C FC RT condition scatters tightly about the 2000 N/mm² gridline. In compression ([112]-oriented, 5×5×10 mm³ specimens, room temperature, 10^-4 s^-1, yield stress as 0.2% proof stress) the stress-strain curve rises steeply through a knee at roughly 1.5–2% strain and then continues as a nearly flat plateau with only slight hardening, running at the low end of the four compared conditions and ending in the 470–480 MPa band at about 5.5% strain. Prior heat treatment changes the flow stress of these monocrystals only modestly; the largest, still small, increase came from quenching from 1100 °C plus 300 °C/14 d annealing. Characterisation techniques applied to this material were ICP analysis (composition), the laser light-figure orientation method, optical metallography after etching in alcoholic 10% nitric acid, SEM with EDX (fracture surfaces, inclusion analysis), microhardness testing and compression testing.
summary: This is a (111)- and [112]-oriented monocrystalline binary Fe-16 at.% Al sample that was annealed at 1100 °C and then furnace cooled to room temperature ("1100 °C FC RT"). It is a terminal-heat-treatment state deliberately chosen as a near-equilibrium (minimum-degree-of-order) reference in a study of how quenching, annealing and short-range ordering affect the low-temperature deformation behaviour of iron-rich Fe-Al alloys. Its room-temperature universal hardness is ≈2000 N/mm² and its [112]-oriented compressive flow curve plateaus at ≈470–480 MPa at ≈5.5% strain.
unmapped: The same Fe-16%Al monocrystal type served two orientations: (111)-oriented specimens for the microhardness (HU) measurements and [112]-oriented 5×5×10 mm³ specimens for the compression tests; this orientation difference should be kept in mind when comparing hardness and flow-stress values.

Rare globular AlN inclusions up to 30 µm in diameter were identified in the monocrystals by EDX analysis, and optical/SEM metallography confirmed that no carbides form in this low-carbon (45 ppm) Fe-16%Al crystal.

The paper reports that the study's results contrast with Davies' earlier finding of a 25% yield-stress increase in a quenched Fe-16.5%Al alloy after a 1 h anneal at 300 °C, which the authors attribute to differences in alloy preparation/impurity content.

TEM dislocation-substructure comparisons (quenched vs furnace-cooled states showing glide bands, tangles and cell formation) were performed on polycrystalline Fe-12%Al and Fe-16%Al (with <20 ppm C), not on this monocrystal; they support the mechanisms discussed but are not direct observations of the present sample.
